draft.title: Parody, pastiche and homage
card: copies the style of a text or genre in order to mock it. The humour comes from exaggerating features until they look silly.
imitates the style of a text, writer or genre in a playful way. It copies the style for fun and does not aim to mock it.
borrows from a text, such as a scene, a character or a line, to honour it. It shows respect for the original and the writer.
To tell them apart, ask what the writer does with the original. Mocking it points to parody, playing with its style points to pastiche, and honouring it points to homage.
draft.remember: Parody mocks, pastiche plays, homage honours.

a.q: A student writes a story in the grand, gloomy style of an old gothic novel. She loves the style and wants to have fun with it, not mock it. What is it?
a.why: She imitates a style playfully, with no aim to mock it, so it is a pastiche. It is not a parody, because a parody copies a style in order to mock it.
a.clue: Is the writer mocking the style or just playing in it?

b.q: A film ends with a quiet scene that deliberately recreates a famous scene from an older film. The director says it is a tribute to the filmmaker who inspired her. What is this?
b.why: The director borrows a scene from an older film to honour it and its maker, so it is an homage. A pastiche imitates a style for fun, but here the aim is respect for one particular work.
b.clue: Think about why the director borrows the scene.
